A poet and thinker who became the first president of Senegal, from 1960 to 1980. Born in the coastal town of Joal, he studied in Paris and in 1935 became the first African to pass the agrégation, France's top teaching exam.

In Paris in the 1930s he and the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire founded Négritude, a literary movement that celebrated Black African culture and identity against French colonial ideas of assimilation. His own poems are its best known works.

He was taken prisoner fighting for France in 1940. After the war he sat in the French National Assembly as a deputy for Senegal, then part of French West Africa. He led Senegal to independence in 1960, after the short-lived Mali Federation with what is now Mali broke up.

As president he followed a moderate African socialism and kept close ties with France. He stepped down by choice in 1980, rare in Africa then, handing over to Abdou Diouf. In 1983 he became the first African member of the Académie française.
